```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(DeCovarT)
```

The bivariate toy confirms the theoretical benefit of covariance
modelling in a transparent setting but cannot demonstrate realistic
gene-regulatory network (GRN) topology. This scenario uses $G = 20$
genes and $J = 3$ cell types in which types 1 and 2 are **mean-collinear**
($\cos(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot 1},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot 2})=0.9$): the
network topology encoded in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ is the remaining
discriminative signal. Construction, ADEMP benchmark, and the static
network figure live in a **single** script,
`scripts/fig03_variance_covariance_driven.R` (seed `20260807`).

# Generative model {#sec-scenario-grid}

One fixed mean signature $\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times J}$ is
built with `generate_mean_signature_matrix()` and an explicit Gram
`target_gram` ([mean signature
construction](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#sec-lr-block-mu)).
There is no marker block and no null (`equal_all`) block: uninformative
genes would be removed before deconvolution.

$$
R
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0.9 & 0.1 \\
0.9 & 1 & 0.1 \\
0.1 & 0.1 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}
=
s\mathbf{Q}R^{1/2},
\quad s=10.
$$ {#eq-fig03-gram}

Because $\mathbf{Q}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{I}_J$, the pairwise
cosines of the columns of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ equal $R$ exactly (up to
rounding). Euclidean gaps follow
$\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot k}\rVert
=s\sqrt{2(1-R_{jk})}$. The call uses `nonnegative = TRUE` (disjoint
gene-block frame) so that $\boldsymbol{\mu}\ge 0$, as required by
`deconvolute_ratios()`.

| pair | cosine | Euclidean |
|:-----|-------:|----------:|
| celltype_1 vs celltype_2 | 0.9 | $10\sqrt{0.2}\approx 4.472$ |
| celltype_1 vs celltype_3 | 0.1 | $10\sqrt{1.8}\approx 13.416$ |
| celltype_2 vs celltype_3 | 0.1 | $10\sqrt{1.8}\approx 13.416$ |

: Exact pairwise geometry of the $20\times 3$ mean signature (`target_gram`, `mean_scale` $=10$). {#tbl-mean-geometry}

Each of the mean-collinear types (CT1, CT2) independently draws an
undirected skeleton from one of two generators, then completes a signed
precision with
`build_normalised_precision()`
([GGM networks](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#sec-ggm-networks);
topology families in
[the topology table](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#tbl-topologies)):

- **Scale-free** (`graph_model = "scale_free"`): Barabási–Albert
  preferential attachment (`power = 1`, `edges_per_node = 1`).
- **Cluster / stochastic block model**
  (`graph_model = "stochastic_block_model"`): three blocks with
  probabilities $(0.5,0.25,0.25)$, $p_{\mathrm{within}}=0.25$,
  $p_{\mathrm{between}}=0.01$.

Erdős–Rényi is not used. Type 3, already separated by the Gram
($R_{13}=R_{23}=0.1$), is held at scale-free, so the topology factorial
is $2^{2}=4$ assignments on CT1 and CT2. Those generator names and
parameter lists are stored on every row of the `config` element of
`output/fig03/fig03_benchmark.rds` as `graph_ct1` / `graph_ct2` /
`graph_ct3` and the list-column `graph_generators`; the true moments
of each scenario are in its `theta_true` element.

The spectral cushion $u$ used at completion is now a **fixed**
engineering constant (`PRECISION_SHIFT_BASE = 0.2`) so that each
graph has one SPD precision. The experimental knob is a global
covariance scale $s$: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\mapsto s\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$
keeps every structural zero of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j$ because
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j(s)=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j/s$.
`scale_covariances_to_overlap()` searches $s$ so that MixSim
`BarOmega` matches a target in $\{0.02,0.08,0.20\}$ (low / moderate /
high), using Sobol Monte Carlo for $G=20$
([overlap note](theory-distance-covariance.html#sec-fig03-scale)).
This is the graph-constrained analogue of MixSim / FSDA average-overlap
simulation
([CRAN MixSim](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MixSim/refman/MixSim.html#MixSim);
[@melnykovMixSimPackageSimulating2012; @rianiSimulatingMixturesMultivariate2015]):
we do **not** call `MixSim()` as a generator, because it cannot take
a precision support as input.

Larger $s$ also raises the covariance-information fraction
$f_{\mathrm{cov}}$ (mean Fisher scales as $1/s$; the covariance block
is scale-invariant). See the
[tangent-Fisher callout](theory-synthetic-scenarios-mean-covariance.html#nte-desc-fisher).

| Factor | Levels |
|---|---|
| Graph model (CT1, CT2) | scale-free; cluster SBM |
| Graph model (CT3) | scale-free (fixed) |
| Target `BarOmega` | low ($0.02$); moderate ($0.08$); high ($0.20$) |
| Topology assignments | $2^{2}=\mathbf{4}$ |
| Covariance draws | $4\times 3=\mathbf{12}$ |

: Covariance factorial (graphs $\times$ target average overlap). {#tbl-cov-factorial}

`describe_simulation_scenario()` records the realised `BarOmega`,
$f_{\mathrm{cov}}$, $\kappa\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})\}$, and
pairwise AIRM distance of the $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ on every row.
The overlap target is matched at the **balanced** composition;
unbalanced $\boldsymbol{p}$ change MixSim's MAP weights, so realised
`BarOmega` is higher there. AIRM is invariant to the global scale
$s$ (it scores topology / shape). $f_{\mathrm{cov}}$ rises with $s$.

![Two generator examples on $G=20$ nodes (scale-free, cluster SBM).
Mean-collinear cell types 1 and 2 are each assigned one of these
families; type 3 is held at scale-free.](figures/fig_network_topologies.png){#fig-network-topologies width="100%"}

Two generators were considered but not adopted:

- **Toeplitz covariances**: encode only local (banded) dependencies;
  cannot model cell-type-specific sparse precision.
- **`MixSim()` as a mixture generator**: draws unconstrained means and
  covariances for a target average overlap; no graph-constrained
  precision input. DeCovarT keeps the graphs and matches `BarOmega`
  by scaling $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ instead.

# Inference {#sec-hybrid-deconvolution}

Compositions are one-dominant vectors from
`composition_from_entropy()` targeting normalised Shannon entropy
$H^{\star}\in\{1,0.5,0.1\}$ (balanced; moderately unbalanced; highly
unbalanced). All DeCovarT solvers start at the barycentre
(`initial_p = "barycentre"`). Other initialisation strategies are
reserved for separate scenarios.

| Factor | Levels |
|---|---|
| Composition $\boldsymbol{p}$ | $H^{\star}=1$; $H^{\star}=0.5$; $H^{\star}=0.1$ |
| **Total scenarios** | $4\times 3\times 3=\mathbf{36}$ |

: Composition factor. {#tbl-composition-factor}

The run size is hard-coded at the top of the script:

| Constant | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `N_REPLICATES` | Monte Carlo bulks per scenario, $N$ | 200 |
| `N_REFERENCE` | individuals of the reference panel, $R$ (MEAD and RNA-Sieve) | 200 |
| `CORES` | workers for the $N$ bulks of a scenario; the three figure scripts run at the same time | a third of half the cores (14 of 88) |
| `POSTPROCESS_ONLY` | `TRUE` redraws the figures from the saved benchmark | `FALSE` |

: Run-size constants of `scripts/fig03_variance_covariance_driven.R`. {#tbl-run-size}

Parallel workers load the **installed** DeCovarT, so run
`devtools::install()` before a parallel run.

## Methods {#sec-hybrid-methods}

Every method is scored on the same simulated bulks. Feature selection
is switched off everywhere: all $G=20$ genes enter every fit.

| Method | Function or code | Input | Intervals |
|:-------|:-----------------|:------|:----------|
| `lsei` (DeconRNASeq) | `deconvolute_ratios_deconrnaseq()` | true means | none |
| NNLS | `deconvolute_ratios_nnls()` | true means | none |
| RLM (robust linear model) | `deconvolute_ratios_rlm()` | true means | none |
| CIBERSORT ($\nu$-SVR) | `deconvolute_ratios_cibersort()` | true means | none |
| Newton–Raphson | `deconvolute_ratios_Newton_Raphson()` | true moments | Wald, ILR, profile, oracle |
| L-BFGS-B | `deconvolute_ratios_L_BFGS_B()` | true moments | Wald, ILR, profile |
| Firth | `fit_firth_decovart()` | true moments | Wald, ILR |
| MEAD | `MEAD::MEAD()` (GitHub, commit `d66fa10`) | reference panel, cohort of $N$ bulks | native sandwich interval |
| RNA-Sieve | `rnasieve` 0.1.4 (Python) | reference panel, cohort of $N$ bulks | released, Fisher and Godambe (see below) |
| ReDeconv | `redeconv` 1.2.1 (Python) | true means and standard deviations | none |

: Methods of the covariance-driven benchmark. {#tbl-solver-hybrid}

- **`lsei` and NNLS.** NNLS followed by renormalisation is least squares
  on the simplex with a **free** scale ($\boldsymbol\beta=c\boldsymbol p$,
  $c=\mathbf 1^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$); `lsei` fixes $c=1$. They agree
  only when $\hat c=1$. In population scenarios the true scale is 1, so
  `lsei` uses information NNLS discards; both are run, to show the
  difference. On 500 bulks of a design like this one with
  $\boldsymbol p=(0.84,0.08,0.08)$, the largest coordinate difference
  between the two has median $0.03$, 95th percentile $0.11$ and maximum
  $0.19$.
- **L-BFGS-B** runs on the closure chart $\boldsymbol p=\boldsymbol w/\mathbf
  1^{\top}\boldsymbol w$ with the box $\boldsymbol w\ge 0$
  ([closure chart](theory-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-closure-box)):
  it maximises the convolution likelihood itself, reaches exact zeros,
  and its box KKT points are the simplex KKT points.
- **Firth** maximises the Jeffreys-penalised likelihood
  [@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993]; its estimate is the same for both
  optimisers, so it appears once.
- **Second-generation methods** run from their authors' code, with gene
  selection and preprocessing filters off and the other defaults kept
  (`scripts/benchmark_metrics/second_generation_methods.R`; the Python
  ones through a `uv` project in `scripts/benchmark_metrics/python/`,
  exchanging CSV files with R). MEAD and RNA-Sieve read a reference
  panel of $R$ purified profiles per type drawn **independently** of the
  bulks (`simulate_reference_replicates()`, its own seed), and are fitted
  on the cohort of the $N$ bulks of a scenario, whereas DeCovarT fits
  one bulk at a time.
  - MEAD rescales every reference profile to a unit total, so its
    proportions are transcript fractions; its intervals are scored
    against both the cell and the transcript fractions.
  - The released interval code of RNA-Sieve returns $[0,1]$ whenever its
    averaged Hessian has a condition number above $10^{6}$ (`stats.py`,
    lines 224 and 234 of version 0.1.4): it then computes
    $\boldsymbol H\boldsymbol B\boldsymbol H^{\top}$ instead of
    $\boldsymbol H^{-1}\boldsymbol B\boldsymbol H^{-\top}$ on a gene
    subsample. The runner also returns the two intervals of the paper,
    recomputed on all genes with the package's own per-gene scores and
    averaged Hessian: Fisher ($\boldsymbol B^{-1}/G$, the empirical Fisher
    information) and Godambe
    ($\boldsymbol H^{-1}\boldsymbol B\boldsymbol H^{-\top}/G$), with
    $\alpha_K=1-\sum_{k<K}\alpha_k$. In the latest dry run the faulty
    branch never fired, so the released and Godambe intervals coincide;
    RNA-Sieve's solver converged in all 36 scenarios of that run, but
    failed in one to three of them in earlier draws (recorded as a
    numerical failure, a grey tile in the heatmaps).
  - DECALS has no public implementation and is not run; its point
    estimate, constrained least squares solved as a quadratic programme,
    is the `lsei` baseline.

## Interval constructions {#sec-hybrid-intervals}

| Interval | Construction |
|:---------|:-------------|
| `wald` | delta method on $\boldsymbol p$, symmetric |
| `ilr` | Wald interval in ILR coordinates mapped back to the simplex |
| `profile` | likelihood-ratio inversion; chart-invariant, inside $[0,1]$ |
| `oracle` | $\hat p_j\pm$ the Wald half-width at $\boldsymbol p^{\star}$ (Fisher at the truth) |

: Interval menu ([population inference](theory-population-inference.html)). {#tbl-interval-menu}

Coverage is reported with a Wilson Monte Carlo interval
[@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019]; the interval table also gives the
mean and median width and the share of intervals leaving $[0,1]$.

```{r}
#| label: inference
benchmark <- readRDS("output/fig03/fig03_benchmark.rds")
names(benchmark)
#> meta config theta_true descriptors supplementary regression
#> monte_carlo optimisation intervals data
dplyr::filter(benchmark$intervals, is_composition) |>
  dplyr::select(ID, algorithm, ci_method, parameter, coverage, mean_width)
```

## Two-dimensional projections of a Gaussian convolution {#sec-hybrid-2d-proj}

With $G=20$ the purified Gaussians and the bulk convolution are no
longer drawable in the gene plane. `latent_projections.pdf` maps each
selected scenario (lowest and highest overlap, balanced and highly
unbalanced composition, four graph assignments) to two planes.

::: {#nte-conv-not-gmm .callout-warning}
A $J$-type bulk draw is
$Y\mid\boldsymbol{p}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}(\boldsymbol{p}),\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr)$
with
$\boldsymbol{\mu}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$.
Every observation is a weighted sum of **all** types
([`simulate_bulk_mixture()`](../reference/simulate_bulk_mixture.html)).
A finite mixture instead draws a latent label and then one
component,
$f(\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_k\pi_k\,\phi(\boldsymbol{y};\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$,
with mixing weights $\boldsymbol{p}$ (not $\boldsymbol{p}^2$).
`MclustDR` targets that mixture. Its $\pi_k$ are not cell-type
proportions, and its component densities are not the convolution law
used for deconvolution.
:::

### Principal components of the purified profiles

Principal components of the pooled purified draws, coloured by type,
show what the **means** alone separate: types 1 and 2, whose means
have cosine $0.9$, overlap on the first two components, while type 3
stands apart.

### Supervised `MclustDR` plane

The second panel fits `mclust::MclustDA(..., modelType = "EDDA")` to the
labelled purified draws, then `mclust::MclustDR()`
[@R-mclust; @scruccaDimensionReductionModelbased2010a;
@scruccaGraphicalToolsModelbased2015]
([`MclustDR` reference](https://mclust-org.github.io/mclust/reference/MclustDR.html)).
Its kernel combines the separation of the class means with the
differences of the class covariances, which is the signal DeCovarT
exploits. Its generalised eigenvalues measure class-relevant
variability, not ordinary PCA variance. The panels with independent
factor analyses (Thomson scores) and mixtures of common factor
analysers were dropped: they described each type, or an unlabelled
mixture, but not the contrast between types.

## Solver runtime and memory {#sec-hybrid-resources}

`runtime.pdf` and `memory.pdf` use the same composition order as
the other performance books (balanced, then moderately unbalanced,
then highly unbalanced): **one page per** \(\boldsymbol{p}\). Each page
facets the three MixSim overlap levels, puts CT1/CT2 topology on
the x-axis (`SF/SF`, `SF/SBM`, `SBM/SF`, `SBM/SBM`), and maps
solver to colour, fill, and grouping. The geometry is a vertical
ggdist half-eye (raincloud) of the per-sample
`optimisation$elapsed_sec` or `memory_bytes` (converted to MiB),
with a left-side `geom_rug()` of the raw Monte Carlo draws and a
log10 y-axis.

## Likelihood geometry and solver behaviour {#sec-hybrid-findings}

::: {.callout-note}
The numbers in this section come from the archived run of
`output/archives/fig03/` ($N=50$, Wald intervals only), which still
included Marquardt–Levenberg and the earlier L-BFGS-B that renormalised
a box-constrained fit. They will be replaced by those of the production
run; the mechanisms they illustrate do not depend on the solver list.
:::

Cell types 1 and 2 share cosine $0.9$, so the mean map
$\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ is close to singular in the
$(p_1,p_2)$ plane: type 3 is the only well-separated mean. MixSim
$\bar\omega$ then sets how much of the remaining signal lives in
$\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}$. The pack in
`output/fig03/mle_explanation/` (descriptors, ILR slices of $\ell$ at
$\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}^{\star}$, expected-Fisher SEs,
Newton/Marquardt forests on **balanced** compositions, and a
quantile-sampled raincloud across all $H^{\star}$) is the numerical
reading of that geometry. As in the bivariate toy, three layers must be
kept apart: the convolution $\ell$, the surrogate each solver
optimises, and the chart / KKT / stopping rule.

### Surrogates versus the convolution

`lsei` (`limSolve`) is again a convex QP for
$\|\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}\|_2^2$ on the simplex
[@R-limSolve; @gongDeconRNASeqStatisticalFramework2013;
@dessoleLawsonHansonAlgorithmDeviation2023;
@boydConvexOptimization2004]. With two nearly collinear
signature columns the QP is under-determined in the $(p_1,p_2)$
direction; the equality $\sum p_j=1$ plus bounds then put mass on a
face. `CIBERSORT` replaces squares by a $\nu$-SVR hinge
[@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015]. The dual is a convex quadratic
programme solved by sequential working-set methods
[@fanWorkingSetSelection2005]. The wrapper
does **not** constrain coefficients to the simplex during the fit:
negatives are clipped to zero and the remainder is renormalised. Clipping
is a Euclidean projection onto the positive orthant, not a constrained
MLE, so a support vector that overshoots becomes a vertex of
$\Delta^{2}$. Neither method sees $p_j^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$.

DeCovarT solvers maximise the Gaussian convolution. `Newton-Raphson`
and `Marquardt-Levenberg` do so in ILR, with a full Hessian versus
Marquardt damping plus RDM
[@marquardtAlgorithmLeastSquaresEstimation1963;
@commengesNewtonLikeAlgorithmLikelihood2006;
@philippsRobustEfficientOptimization2021; @R-marqLevAlg]. `L-BFGS-B`
uses a limited-memory inverse Hessian on the closure chart
$\boldsymbol p=\boldsymbol w/\mathbf 1^{\top}\boldsymbol w$, $\boldsymbol w\ge0$
[@byrdLimitedMemoryAlgorithm1995; @zhuAlgorithm778LBFGSB1997]. The
same caveats as in
[the bivariate interpretation](fig02-bivariate-toy.html#sec-bivariate-findings)
apply: Boyd's local-quadratic Newton rate needs a locally strongly
concave $\ell$; RDM stops when further ILR steps are smaller than
statistical error; the archived box-constrained BFGS, which
renormalised a free-scale fit, could sit on a face that is not a
stationary point of $\ell$ (the closure chart now used cannot). All of this is still $N=1$ per bulk
([finite-sample MLE](theory-population-inference.html#sec-finite-sample)).

### Balanced compositions (forest + Fisher)

The Newton/Marquardt forest in the pack is restricted to
$H^{\star}=1$ ($p^{\star}=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$). On that slice the two
second-order solvers are interchangeable. At low overlap (`V1`, both
graphs scale-free) RMSE for $p_1$ is $0.113$, bias $0.012$, empirical
SD $0.113$, coverage $0.99$. At high overlap (`V7`) RMSE rises only to
$0.124$ and coverage stays $0.99$. Median RMSE for $p_1$ across the
four graph assignments is $0.122$ (low $\bar\omega$), $0.134$
(moderate), $0.147$ (high); type 3, whose mean is not collinear, stays
easier at low overlap (median RMSE $0.064$) and catches up as overlap
grows ($0.130$). Expected-Fisher ILR standard errors in
`theoretical_wald_se.csv` tell the same story:
$\mathrm{SE}_{\rho_1}$ goes from $0.63$ (`V1`) to $0.97$ (`V7`), and
the condition number of the ILR information drops from $6.8$ to $1.7$
— not because the problem becomes better posed, but because *both*
eigenvalues shrink and the ellipsoid becomes a large, round disk.
Graph assignment (scale-free versus cluster SBM) moves those SEs by a
smaller amount than $\bar\omega$ does. Topology is visible;
**average overlap is the dominant knob**, matching the design claim,
for *balanced* $p^{\star}$ and for *second-order convolution MLEs*.

### Boundary pile-up (raincloud, all $H^{\star}$)

The sampled raincloud (`raincloud_sampled.csv`) includes moderately and
highly unbalanced Shannon targets. Among non-missing point estimates,
$76\%$ of `CIBERSORT` values lie at $0$ or $1$. At the scenario-wise
median (`sample_role = q50`), type 3 is exactly zero in $35$ of $36$
scenarios (mean $\hat p_3=0.0008$). That is the clip-and-renormalise
step, not a convolution mode on a face. `lsei` sits on a bound in
$42\%$ of sampled cells overall and in $58\%$ of highly unbalanced
cells; `LBFGS` in $26\%$ and $36\%$; Marquardt in $10\%$ and $17\%$;
Newton in $4\%$ and $12\%$. On balanced raincloud rows Newton and
Marquardt never hit $\{0,1\}$; LSEI still does ($21\%$). Mean-only and
SVR methods convert a collinear mean map into a **hard** boundary
estimate; ILR convolution methods convert it into a **soft** interior
mode, until $p^{\star}$ itself is a rare-type vertex.

Median absolute error of the $q_{50}$ $p_1$ fit across scenarios is
$0.048$ (Newton), $0.100$ (`lsei`), $0.114$ (`LBFGS`), $0.142$
(Marquardt), $0.159$ (`CIBERSORT`). The Marquardt figure is not a
contradiction of the balanced forest: on the highly unbalanced scenario
`V3` ($p^{\star}\approx(0.980,0.010,0.010)$) the $q_{50}$ estimates are
$0.92$ (Newton), $0.93$ (`lsei`), $1.00$ (`CIBERSORT`), $0.82$
(`LBFGS`), and $0.78$ (Marquardt). LSEI is closer to the vertex because
the QP *wants* a vertex; Marquardt is pulled toward the barycentre
because RDM refuses a long ILR walk, the same mechanism as `B811` in
the bivariate pack. Covariance information therefore helps only if the
solver actually follows the convolution ridge to the rare-type
coordinate. A mean-only vertex can beat a damped interior MLE on raw
$p_1$ error when the truth is already a vertex; it will still report
$\hat p_3=0$ and cannot support a chi-bar-square test that the type is
absent ([boundary inference](theory-population-inference.html#sec-boundary)).

### Ridges in the ILR slices

`ilr_loglik_profiles.csv` slices $\ell(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ at
$\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}^{\star}$. High $\bar\omega$
produces ridges along the type-1/type-2 contrast (the collinear mean
direction): many $(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ give almost the same convolution
Gaussian. Newton follows the ridge until the Hessian in the remaining
well-identified direction (type 3 versus $\{1,2\}$) stops it. Marquardt
stops earlier when RDM sees no inferential gain. `L-BFGS-B`, stepping
in $p$ with only box bounds, can leave the simplex during the line
search and land near a face after $p/\sum p$, which is the raincloud's
$26\%$ bound rate. None of these paths is the Godambe sandwich or a
Firth penalty [@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993]; the Firth fit is now
benchmarked as its own method
([Firth](theory-population-inference.html#sec-firth)).
With $N=1$, the honest frequentist statement for a rare type is still
the restricted LRT / parametric bootstrap of the MLE article, not a
Wald ellipse from `vcov_ilr_delta()`.
